text.tspan: International cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI) regulation between the European
Union and the United States faces two fundamental structural barriers that conventional
institutional design cannot readily overcome. The first is an information and enforcement
problem: AI systems are opaque by nature, preventing regulators from verifying compliance
with any agreement that might be reached. The second is a domestic political divergence:
the U.S. prioritizes innovation and resists heavy-handed regulation, while the EU centers
its approach on users' rights and precautionary governance, producing incompatible
institutional preferences with almost no overlap in acceptable rules.
Drawing on the analytical framework of Professor James D. Morrow's POLSCI 160 course,
this paper argues that these barriers make a binding international AI regulatory institution
unlikely in the foreseeable future. Cooperation will instead remain confined to soft law:
voluntary commitments, shared technical standards, and non-binding guidelines.

g.text: Keywords: artificial intelligence governance, international cooperation, EU AI Act,
soft law, domestic politics, enforcement, U.S.-EU relations
